title: Cavity-Mediated Charging of a Graphene Excitonic Quantum Battery
abstract: We study the charging and work-extraction properties of a graphene-based excitonic quantum battery embedded in a driven-dissipative optical microcavity. The system consists of a pair of intervalley excitons in strained graphene, where one exciton acts as the charger and the other as the quantum battery, both coupled to a common cavity mode through a Tavis-Cummings interaction. By solving the open-system dynamics, we analyze the ergotropy as a measure of extractable work and investigate how coherent and incoherent pumping, cavity loss, and the microcavity parameter influence the charging process. Our results show that the battery exhibits a transient ergotropy peak followed by relaxation to a steady state, with the maximum extractable work strongly controlled by the light-matter coupling strength. The study reveals an optimal regime for efficient charging and demonstrates the role of cavity engineering in enhancing work storage in excitonic quantum batteries.
summary: The paper models a graphene-based excitonic quantum battery coupled to an optical microcavity to study its charging efficiency. By analyzing the system's dynamics using ergotropy, the authors determine that optimal energy storage requires balancing external coherent pumping against cavity dissipation. This work highlights how cavity engineering can enhance the usable work capacity of such solid-state quantum devices.
main_problem: The study investigates how efficiently energy can be stored and extracted from a quantum battery implemented using excitons coupled to an optical cavity.
main_result: The maximum extractable work (ergotropy) is strongly controlled by the light-matter coupling strength, and optimal charging occurs when coherent pumping balances cavity dissipation near a specific ratio.
method: The authors solve the open-system dynamics using a master equation approach to model energy flow in the driven-dissipative system.
model_or_system: The physical system is a pair of intervalley excitons in strained graphene acting as a quantum battery, coupled via Tavis-Cummings interaction to a common optical microcavity mode.
key_observables: Ergotropy (measure of extractable work), transient ergotropy peak ($W_{	ext{max}}$), and steady-state ergotropy ($W_{	ext{ss}}$).
important_parameters: Light-matter coupling strength, cavity loss ($\gamma_c$), pumping strength ratio ($	ext{RP}/\gamma_c$), and the pseudomagnetic field parameter ($B$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes low exciton density, neglecting direct exciton-exciton interactions, and that the cavity remains resonant with the excitonic transition.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the coupling of two excitons to a microcavity mode; subsequent figures compare ergotropy evolution versus pumping ratios and PMF strength.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model (Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonian), derives the open-system master equation incorporating both incoherent and coherent driving, analyzes the resulting dynamics using ergotropy as a diagnostic tool, and finally maps out optimal operating regimes by varying external parameters.
why_interesting: This work sits at the intersection of cavity QED, open quantum systems, and energy storage, providing concrete theoretical guidelines for engineering solid-state quantum devices like excitonic batteries.
